clue.text: Shoulder bag, left by a chest, exploded

indicators.note: something exploded is blown apart, so the letters that follow land in a new order

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A shoulder bag left next to a chest has blown up, like a security alert at a station.
explanation.definitionFit: A satchel is a bag carried by a strap over the shoulder, typically used by schoolchildren.

clue.text: Correct copy reveals plot in case

indicators.note: in places the plot inside the case, which wraps around it

parts.note: a suit is a case brought in a law court
a plot of garden ground is a bed

explanation.surface: A legal transcript exposes a conspiracy within a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' sounds like a scheme, but it is a garden plot.
explanation.definitionFit: To subedit is to check and correct copy for publication, the job of a newspaper subeditor.

clue.text: Story about British food

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the story wraps around the abbreviation that follows

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A report about British cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Food' is fair because a house that 'keeps a good table' serves good meals.
explanation.definitionFit: Table can mean the food provided at meals, as in a hotel that keeps an excellent table.

clue.text: Ridiculous, as an underdone loaf may be

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ill-conceived, poorly thought out

definitions.text: as an underdone loaf may be
definitions.meaning: second meaning: literally only partly cooked in the oven

explanation.walkthrough: The second half takes the figurative word literally: bread that has spent only part of its time in the oven.
explanation.definitionFit: A half-baked idea is foolish and poorly planned; a half-baked loaf is literally undercooked.

clue.text: Fabulous creature with horns — closest men petrified

indicators.note: petrified people shake in terror, so these words are scrambled into fresh order

explanation.surface: A horned beast terrifies the men nearest to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fabulous' means from fable, not marvellous: the creature is a legend of a Scottish lake.
explanation.definitionFit: The Loch Ness Monster is a legendary creature said to live in Loch Ness in the Scottish Highlands.

clue.text: Skegness finally got hotter, and crowded

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the place name before it, keeping only its closing letter

parts.note: to get hotter is to warm up

explanation.surface: A hot day at Skegness, a Lincolnshire seaside resort, finally brings the crowds to the beach.
explanation.definitionFit: To swarm a place is to throng it in great numbers, so swarmed is a synonym of crowded.

clue.text: Plain sailing? Right on!

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for the adjective sense: easy, uncomplicated
definitions.meaning: first meaning: simple and free of difficulty
second meaning: read as two words, directly ahead

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right on!' looks like a cheer of approval; split the answer into two words and it means continuing directly ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: Something uncomplicated is plain sailing; straight forward, as two words, describes going right on ahead.

clue.text: Greek character employed by local pharmacist

indicators.note: employed by means taken on inside, so the answer sits within the following words

parts.note: found spanning the end of local and the start of pharmacist

explanation.surface: A Greek person works for the neighbourhood chemist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person, but it is a letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, a Greek character in the written sense.

clue.text: Two doctors describing swimming race close to Lancashire resort town

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round, so the doctors surround the jumbled word

parts.note: MO (medical officer) and MB (Bachelor of Medicine) are both abbreviations for doctors

indicators.note: swimming suggests movement, so the following word's letters drift into new positions
the close of a word is its final letter, which is all that is kept

explanation.surface: Two medics report on a swimming contest near a north-west England resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to Lancashire' looks like a location, but it simply means the county's last letter; the definition is just 'resort town', though Lancashire is where it lies.
explanation.definitionFit: Morecambe is a seaside holiday destination on Morecambe Bay in Lancashire, north-west England.

clue.text: Absolutely determined, clique departed earlier

indicators.note: earlier tells us the word for departed comes before the one for clique

parts.note: a set is a social group or clique

explanation.surface: A group whose members have left are thoroughly resolved.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead set, as in dead set on going, means utterly resolved and unwilling to change one's mind.

clue.text: Be excited about a run in vehicle

parts.note: to bubble is to be full of excitement
C is short for circa, Latin for about
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: Someone thrilled at the prospect of going for a drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container signal but here it just supplies the abbreviation for circa.
explanation.definitionFit: A bubble car is a tiny domed microcar of the 1950s and 60s, such as the Isetta, so it is a kind of vehicle.

clue.text: Windproof jacket used by old man protecting chest

indicators.note: to protect something is to wrap around it, so the old man surrounds the chest

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man
an ark is an old word for a chest or coffer

explanation.surface: An elderly man wears a windproof jacket to keep his chest warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chest' reads as part of the body, but it is a box, the old sense of ark.
explanation.definitionFit: A parka is a hooded weatherproof coat, originally an Inuit garment, made to keep out wind.

clue.text: Nerd starts to dismantle Wankel engines, each bit

indicators.note: starts are the opening letters, so each following word gives only its initial

explanation.surface: A geek begins taking a rotary Wankel engine apart, piece by piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Dweeb is American slang for a socially awkward, studious person, much the same as a nerd.

clue.text: Pests cause inns to be refurbished

indicators.note: refurbishing a building rearranges its parts, so the preceding letters are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: Vermin are forcing pubs to close for renovation.
explanation.definitionFit: Pests are people or creatures that annoy, which is exactly what nuisances are.

clue.text: Money no object making an Astaire film?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: there is no limit on what can be spent
second meaning: a 1943 musical starring Fred Astaire

explanation.surface: A lavish budget lets a studio produce a Fred Astaire picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the film is identified by its title alone; it is a wartime RKO musical with Joan Leslie.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means there is no upper limit, which is what money no object conveys, and it is also the film's exact title.

clue.text: Number joining groups taking time off for morning coffee

indicators.note: taking something away removes it, here working with off to strip the abbreviation from the groups
off means removed, so the abbreviation for time is taken out of the groups

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A worker joins colleagues during a mid-morning break for coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: Elevenses is a British mid-morning snack or drink, taken around eleven o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevenses is a light mid-morning break, typically with coffee or tea, named for the hour.

clue.text: I see what you're saying

parts.note: surface reading: a casual phrase meaning I understand you; setter's reading: literally, I watch your words being formed on your mouth

explanation.walkthrough: The everyday idiom for understanding is taken literally: someone who follows speech by watching mouth movements.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who follows speech by watching mouth movements, often deaf, literally sees what is said.

clue.text: More cheesed off, alarmingly, about president defining a civil right

indicators.note: about means around, so the shuffled phrase goes round the head of state
something done alarmingly is wild and disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for president

explanation.surface: Citizens grow ever more fed up with a head of state, while describing a basic liberty.
explanation.walkthrough: The P goes inside the jumble; since every letter is rearranged together, its exact position does not matter. 'Cheesed off' is British slang for annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: The liberty to express opinions without censorship is a fundamental civil right protected in most democracies.

clue.text: Ripped off down end of road

parts.note: down and fleece are both soft, fluffy coverings

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

explanation.surface: Someone was robbed at the bottom of the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' looks like a direction to go with 'end of road', but it is the soft fluff of feathers or wool.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to swindle them, so fleeced is slang for ripped off or overcharged.

clue.text: Bishopric? Yes, possibly in difficult situation

indicators.note: in places the rearranged word inside the predicament

parts.note: to be in a hole is to be in trouble

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible arrangement of the word before it

explanation.surface: Asked if a diocese is in trouble, someone answers yes, possibly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Holy See is the episcopal see of Rome, the Pope's jurisdiction, and a see is a bishopric.

clue.text: Shock when peeper gets key

parts.note: a peeper is a playful word for an eye
a key is something that opens a lock

explanation.surface: A Peeping Tom is startled when handed a key.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye-opener is a surprising revelation, something that comes as a shock.

clue.text: Finished last of lasagna, Italian food

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

explanation.surface: A diner polishes off the last of the lasagne at an Italian meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta is the Italian dough food of which lasagna is one example.

clue.text: Message he reportedly put on front of envelope

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter, so only the initial is kept
something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we want a word that is said the same as one for he

parts.note: he denotes a male, which is pronounced like post

explanation.surface: A man scribbles a note on the front of an envelope.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down-style charade 'put on' means the second piece follows the first: the envelope's initial leads.
explanation.definitionFit: An email is an electronic message sent between computers.

clue.text: Weapon taken from a disorderly crowd climbing on to top of building

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing means going upwards, so the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a mob is an unruly crowd

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

explanation.surface: A rioting crowd grabs a weapon and climbs onto a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: An A-bomb is an atomic bomb, a nuclear weapon.

clue.text: Foremost of carveries requests large barrels

indicators.note: the foremost part of a word is its first letter, so just the initial is taken

explanation.surface: The leading carvery restaurants order beer in large barrels.
explanation.walkthrough: A carvery is a British restaurant serving roast meat carved to order.
explanation.definitionFit: Casks are wooden containers for liquids such as beer or wine, often big ones.

clue.text: Drops rock band, dismissing explosive type of music involved

indicators.note: something involved is caught up inside, so the musical genre is placed within what remains
dismissing someone sends them away, so the explosive is removed from the band's name

parts.note: the Doors were Jim Morrison's American rock band
HE is the abbreviation for high explosive
rap is a genre of music

explanation.surface: A rock group lets go of its explosive style of music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops' looks like a verb about the band, but it is the definition: drops are hinged floor openings, as on a gallows or stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Trapdoors are hinged panels in a floor or stage that open downwards, so each is a drop.

clue.text: Wrongly praised, padre is unlikely to lose heart

indicators.note: something done wrongly is out of its proper order, so the letters that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A clergyman wrongly lauded won't be easily discouraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Padre is' is itself the same seven letters, so the clue doubles up the rearrangement as a bonus; either word set gives the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To despair is to abandon hope, which is what losing heart means.

clue.text: Awfully bad rule, existing for a long time

indicators.note: something done awfully is messed up, so the letters that follow are jumbled

explanation.surface: A dreadful regulation that has stayed on the books for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: Durable means long-lasting, able to endure over a lengthy period.
